zeile.title: Magellan (MGN) High Electronic Temperatures
zeile.summary: Magellan electronics bays ran 20 degrees C. hotter in flight than was anticipated. Contaminants were believed to have off-gassed in flight and accumulated on the thermal tiles, thus increasing solar absorptance. Evaluate vacuum outgassing procedures, and demonstrate system operation at temperatures beyond those expected in flight. For missions to inner planets, the spacecraft system thermal control design should minimize or avoid solar exposure on critical thermal control surfaces.
zeile.content:
Datum: 1993-07-12

Organisation: JPL

Abstract (Volltext):
Magellan electronics bays ran 20 degrees C. hotter in flight than was anticipated. Contaminants were believed to have off-gassed in flight and accumulated on the thermal tiles, thus increasing solar absorptance. Evaluate vacuum outgassing procedures, and demonstrate system operation at temperatures beyond those expected in flight. For missions to inner planets, the spacecraft system thermal control design should minimize or avoid solar exposure on critical thermal control surfaces.

Lesson:
Effects of contamination on critical thermal control surfaces can be more severe than previously assumed, resulting in higher than expected flight temperatures.          The Mariner 10 thermal control concept (a sun pointing spacecraft with a large sun blocking thermal shade) would result in fewer thermal issues than the transient attitude thermal design employed on Magellan.

zeile.title: Mechanism Problems Because of Tight Rigging Tolerances
zeile.summary: Due to extremely tight tolerances, rigging of the Orbiter�s Manipulator Positioning Mechanism (MPM) required the use of instrumentation to set some of the mechanical components. This greatly complicates and lengthens the rigging process. It also increases the risk of failures/problems because of a higher likelihood of the system being improperly adjusted. It also makes the system more susceptible to problems in flight because of thermal and zero-G effects that cannot be screened for during groun [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-17

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Due to extremely tight tolerances, rigging of the Orbiter�s Manipulator Positioning Mechanism (MPM) required the use of instrumentation to set some of the mechanical components. This greatly complicates and lengthens the rigging process. It also increases the risk of failures/problems because of a higher likelihood of the system being improperly adjusted. It also makes the system more susceptible to problems in flight because of thermal and zero-G effects that cannot be screened for during ground checkout. Designs need to be robust enough that rigging tolerances of a few thousandths of an inch are not necessary.

Lesson:
Requiring such tight rigging tolerances on the mechanical components created several problems and made the process of rigging the mechanisms very complex. The team decided that the best way to determine the on-center position of the linkage was by monitoring the load in the drive rod. Theoretically, the load should peak at the on-center position. In order to measure this so that the stop could be set within the required 0.002 inch tolerance, a linear transducer was installed on the drive bellcrank, and strain gauges were attached to the drive rod. Testing on the flight hardware showed that because of friction and other inconsistencies, the location of the peak load varied depending on the speed at which the linkage was cycled and the direction (stow or deploy). The team eventually decided that the on-center position would be based on an average of the positions of the stow and deploy peak loads, weighted toward the stow position. However, the amount of variability in this measurement resulted in some risk that the stop bolt position would not be set within the required range. The design of the hardware should not require this level of accuracy to ensure proper operation. Additionally, the team found that other seemingly minor things had an effect on the performance of the mechanism. It was discovered that the way the pedestal assembly was attached to the test stand made enough of a difference that it caused it to exceed some of the spec limits. This was because of minor deflections in the base plate of the assembly because of how it was secured to the stand. Also, such tight rigging requirements make the system more susceptible to problems in flight. During ground checkout it is not possible to simulate all the conditions the hardware will experience on-orbit. The effects of zero-G and thermal changes cannot be screened for on the ground. During the first few flights after the modified MPM hardware was installed, there were some problems with the performance of the limit switches. Even during prelaunch operations at the pad we found that the limit switches transferred differently than they did during horizontal processing in the Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF). In flight, some of the limit switch indications did not come on during the cycles but then transferred on some time later. These were believed to be because of thermal effects on orbit. Eventually the specification was updated, and the limit switch rigging was relaxed to account for these issues.

zeile.title: Loads from Soft Goods Not Fully Considered During Design of Mechanical Systems
zeile.summary: The effects of soft goods (environmental seals, pressure seals, thermal barriers, etc.) were not fully considered during the design of several of the orbiter mechanical systems. During rerigging efforts at KSC, it was not possible to meet all the requirements in the drawings/specifications because much of the initial rigging was done without the installation of these soft goods. Loads induced by the soft goods prevented the mechanisms from operating within the required ranges. This was most evid [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-04-27 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The effects of soft goods (environmental seals, pressure seals, thermal barriers, etc.) were not fully considered during the design of several of the orbiter mechanical systems. During rerigging efforts at KSC, it was not possible to meet all the requirements in the drawings/specifications because much of the initial rigging was done without the installation of these soft goods. Loads induced by the soft goods prevented the mechanisms from operating within the required ranges. This was most evident during the rerigging of OV-103�s landing gear after the Columbia accident. The design process should ensure that the loads of soft goods are understood and considered. Also, field rigging specifications should be developed to allow for rework of the system postdelivery. Lesson: There were no requirements to verify the seal compression. Proper compression was assumed based on meeting the door-to-structure flushness requirement. There was also no requirement to verify the height of the seals. There was a postflight visual inspection only.

Attempts to adjust the mechanism to obtain the proper seal compression and door position confirmed that the mechanism was not capable of overcoming the loads of the seals and other soft goods without exceeding other parameters of the rigging specification. Ultimately, some parts of the mechanism were instrumented to ensure that the loads in the critical components remained within acceptable limits. In addition, after the STS-114 rerigging effort was complete, small changes in seal or thermal-barrier stiffness (when components were replaced) resulted in unacceptable changes in the door positions. This often resulted in extensive testing and rework in subsequent flows. There were similar problems with other orbiter mechanical systems, including the ingress/egress hatch and External Tank umbilical doors.

Furthermore, when the system was reworked in the field, it was not always possible to comply with the mechanical rigging specifications. The specs were written from a manufacturing perspective, and often the seals and other Thermal Protection System components were not installed. Following the spec in the field was not always practical because it required that the hardware be returned to the original build configuration. This resulted in partial compliance with the specs and the need for material reviews to document deviations from the spec or out-of-spec conditions.

zeile.title: Reduced Torque Output from Electro-Mechanical Actuators
zeile.summary: Reduced torque output of the orbiter�s electromechanical actuators has been a problem for the Shuttle Program. It has resulted in unplanned work to test, remove, and refurbish the actuators. Disassembly and inspection has revealed that the torque reduction is a result of problems with the torque limiters and the motor clutch/brake assemblies in the actuators. Refurbishment is a lengthy process because of the difficulty involved in setting the torque limiter to operate through the required temper [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-04 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): Reduced torque output of the orbiter�s electromechanical actuators has been a problem for the Shuttle Program. It has resulted in unplanned work to test, remove, and refurbish the actuators. Disassembly and inspection has revealed that the torque reduction is a result of problems with the torque limiters and the motor clutch/brake assemblies in the actuators. Refurbishment is a lengthy process because of the difficulty involved in setting the torque limiter to operate through the required temperature range. The next generation of actuators should have a better design, or the mechanical system should be capable of withstanding the maximum output loads of the actuator. Lesson: The torque limiters of the External Tank door actuators were redesigned in the early 1990s because of unacceptable degradation of the disk friction surfaces. The new design was a multidisk ball-ramp setup. When the torque reached a certain value, the ball-ramp design reduced the compression load on the disk stack and allowed the disks to rotate relative to each other (slip). The disks in this particular actuator were made of steel and Vespel. After several years of service with the new torque limiter design, most of the actuators exhibited reduced torque output. Investigation determined that the torque limiter degradation was due to grease contamination of the disk surfaces. Inspection confirmed that excess grease was applied to some of the torque limiter components (bearings) during assembly and eventually migrated to the disk surfaces. However, even after the actuators were refurbished, excess grease was removed, and the grease was cleaned from the disks, the actuators often continued to exhibit torque degradation and show evidence of grease contamination of the disks. Another problem was the amount of effort required to set the torque limiter to slip in the required range when the actuator was being serviced. The value at which the torque limiter slips depends somewhat on the temperature, and the actuator is required to operate with a specified torque output through a large temperature range (over 300 �F). Several rounds of adjustments were needed, each followed by days of testing.

In addition, there was degradation of the motor clutch/brake assemblies in these actuators. Each actuator has two AC motors, each of which interfaces with the gear box differential through a clutch/brake assembly. For redundancy, the actuator will operate on only one motor. When a motor is not operating, the clutch/brake assembly is in the brake mode. A friction disk is spring-loaded against a stator, which locks the input to the differential and disconnects it from the motor. This is necessary so that during single-motor operation, the nonoperating motor input is not back-driven through the differential. When the motor starts up, the assembly switches to clutch mode. A solenoid pulls the disk away from the stator, separating the brake surfaces and engaging the clutch surface of the disk to the motor output. The motor then drives the differential input through the clutch. During tests of the actuators on the vehicle, the torque output varied significantly by motor mode. Since there is a single torque limiter, the point at which it slips should be the same regardless of which motor is operating. This indicated that the clutch/brake assembly was slipping prematurely. Disassembly and inspection confirmed that both the clutch and brake surfaces were worn. There was evidence of scoring on the interfacing surfaces and metallic debris in the assembly.

zeile.title: Re-Certifying An Umbilical After A Modification
zeile.summary: The flight element design agency modified the design of the External Tank Ground Umbilical Carrier Plate, which is used to vent hydrogen. The design changes were considered minor enough that modeling and simulation were deemed sufficient to certify the part for use. During STS-114 launch operations, a camera recorded a cryogenic liquid leaking from the shroud used for purging the umbilical. Because oxygen liquefies before nitrogen, the evidence of liquid caused a concern that oxygen was liquefyi [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-20 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The flight element design agency modified the design of the External Tank Ground Umbilical Carrier Plate, which is used to vent hydrogen. The design changes were considered minor enough that modeling and simulation were deemed sufficient to certify the part for use. During STS-114 launch operations, a camera recorded a cryogenic liquid leaking from the shroud used for purging the umbilical. Because oxygen liquefies before nitrogen, the evidence of liquid caused a concern that oxygen was liquefying from air and posing a risk to launch operation safety. Lesson: GUCP recertification was based on changes made to the GUCP only and did not include the interactions with the ground shroud. No functional testing was performed with the new GUCP QD configuration with the ice suppression shroud.

The GUCP QD modifications did not undergo a complete system-level test because the modifications were deemed passive and there was no change in form/fit/function, despite significant changes in the QD: going from a two-piece casting to a one-piece casting with significantly more surface area. Analysis and thermal models of the component failed to predict the effect in operational conditions. Also, the purge shroud was not adequately investigated during initial conception and testing to determine when gases would begin to mix and nitrogen purge could begin to intrude upon cryogenically chilled surfaces.

The inadequately tested modifications to the GUCP QD and the lack of close observation of vapor drips from the ice suppression shroud nearly caused the launch of STS-114 to be aborted.

zeile.title: Battery Explosion
zeile.summary: A lead acid battery used for emergency generator starting burst and spread surfuric acid within close proximity of the generator. Diesel Generators (stand-by use) are located in a room at the facility that must be accessed by personnel for reasons other than maintenance. Personnel cannot be expected to recognize the presence and potential hazards of dangerous battery failures at undetermined times.  Preventative maintenance schedules will include increased checks and ensure appropriate barriers [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-16

Organisation: IVV

Abstract (Volltext):
A lead acid battery used for emergency generator starting burst and spread surfuric acid within close proximity of the generator. Diesel Generators (stand-by use) are located in a room at the facility that must be accessed by personnel for reasons other than maintenance. Personnel cannot be expected to recognize the presence and potential hazards of dangerous battery failures at undetermined times.  Preventative maintenance schedules will include increased checks and ensure appropriate barriers are purchased and/or constructed to prevent personnel exposure to battery faults for all generators.

Lesson:
Charging a lead-acid battery produces hydrogen and oxygen gasses which creates pressure inside the battery. Battery explosions can occur and have been reported in industry. One conclusion is when one or more cells have a high concentration of hydrogen gas because the vent cap was plugged or defective and did not release the gas effectively an unsafe condition is created. In addition, when electrolyte levels fall below the top of the plates, a low resistive bridge can form at the top of the plates and when current starts to flow, it can cause an arc or spark in one of the cells to intensify that condition. This combination of events ignites the gas, blows the battery case cover off and spatters electrolyte with potentially injuring unaware personnel and to further damage associated equipment.

zeile.title: Magellan In-Flight Solar Array Deployment Indication
zeile.summary: Although shuttle astronauts observed Magellan solar panel deployment, a microswitch failed to provide a “panels-latched” indication. Ensure that telemetry transducers measure the desired function-- not just a related function. Microswitch design should account for the need for overtravel in the actuation stroke. Perform a FMECA early in the spacecraft life cycle.
zeile.content:
Datum: 1993-07-13

Organisation: JPL

Abstract (Volltext):
Although shuttle astronauts observed Magellan solar panel deployment, a microswitch failed to provide a “panels-latched” indication. Ensure that telemetry transducers measure the desired function-- not just a related function. Microswitch design should account for the need for overtravel in the actuation stroke. Perform a FMECA early in the spacecraft life cycle.

Lesson:
Microswitches on Magellan were mounted such that they would detect the position of the solar panels (as opposed to the status of the latching mechanism). As a result, they were just a position indicator and not a "panels latched" indicator.          A marginal microswitch actuation stroke plus zero-g effects can result in failure of the microswitch to close.          Failure Mode Effects and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) is a worthwhile activity and can result in problem workarounds being built into flight sequences ahead of time.

zeile.summary: The ARES I-X did not apply individual wire harness identification sleeves on the electrical wiring. Wire IDs were used in the Space Shuttle Program and were an important part of the Orbiter processing. The wire IDs aided in wire repairs, functional retest, and system fault isolation. Future Space Flight Programs should use wire identification as part of their wire harness fabrication process, or the initial bui [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-13 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The ARES I-X did not apply individual wire harness identification sleeves on the electrical wiring. Wire IDs were used in the Space Shuttle Program and were an important part of the Orbiter processing. The wire IDs aided in wire repairs, functional retest, and system fault isolation. The schedule impacts of not installing wire IDs were evident in the ARES I-X Program. Future Space Flight Programs should use wire identification as part of their wire harness fabrication process, or the initial build installation and ground flight processing will be impacted. Lesson: Wire IDs were used in the Space Shuttle Program and were an important part of the Orbiter processing. The wire IDs aided in wire repairs, functional retest, and system fault isolation. The schedule impacts of not installing wire IDs were evident in the ARES I-X Program. Future Space Flight Programs should use wire identification as part of their wire harness fabrication process, or the initial build installation and ground flight processing will be impacted.

One example of the value of wire harness IDs in the Shuttle Program is the ability to determine the wire function using only the wire ID. A worst-case scenario is wire damage detected during final closeouts, and when post repair requires a functional retest. If the function is unknown, there are two ways to resolve this condition: perform extensive hardware removals to isolate the wire function or perform functional retest of all wires in the harness. A complete functional retest of all the wires in the harness may not be possible if it contains functions that cannot be retested in the vertical configuration. In this case, it would cause flight hardware removals to isolate the function. The removal of flight hardware in final closeouts would likely drive a slip in the planned launch date. Depending on the vehicle design, this issue could result in the de-stack of the vehicle.

The Orbiter has experienced many cases of wire damage just prior to flight, and wire IDs were invaluable in resolving the issues quickly without impacting the planned launch date.

zeile.content: Datum: 2010-05-20 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): Cryogenic propulsion systems use extremely cold propellants and high pressures to achieve the thrust-to-weight ratios required for space vehicles. Leakage from these systems during operation can cause changes in pressure within an enclosed fuselage (such as the Space Shuttle vehicle [SSV]) that are significant enough to be recognized as the initiation of a potentially catastrophic leak. Monitoring for these unexpected changes in pressure can allow detection of a leak in time to abort a launch and possibly prevent damage to or loss of the vehicle. Lesson: Integrity of the SSV MPS/SSME following SSME start must be derived as acceptable based on historical data and satisfaction of prestart requirements. Because there is no real-time leak detection following SSME start, it is possible to allow lift-off with a significant leak occurring.

zeile.title: Local Design vs. COTS Implementation
zeile.summary: Instead of using commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) equipment to replace the ground instrumentation data acquisition system (Permanent Measurement System [PMS]), NASA and its contractor designed the Ground Measurement System (GMS) in-house. As the result of a technology transfer effort, GMS was manufactured by a commercial vendor. The design of GMS was still undergoing changes during its implementation at the pad. Several components of the system never became fully operational. These complications [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-04-25

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Instead of using commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) equipment to replace the ground instrumentation data acquisition system (Permanent Measurement System [PMS]), NASA and its contractor designed the Ground Measurement System (GMS) in-house. As the result of a technology transfer effort, GMS was manufactured by a commercial vendor. The design of GMS was still undergoing changes during its implementation at the pad. Several components of the system never became fully operational. These complications eventually led the Ground Instrumentation department to replace GMS with a COTS implementation (GMS2/CDAS).

Lesson:
It would have been beneficial to capture the end-user�s requirements prior to the design phase. GMS encountered several roadblocks and the need for major design changes during attempts to implement the system. One component of the system, which required many work hours of troubleshooting, never attained full functionality. In addition, one of the advertised benefits of GMS was the ability to locate the signal conditioning and amplifier circuitry near the transducer or measurement device, but this scheme was also fraught with problems and proved extremely hard to implement in the launch environment. Another weakness observed was the lack of continuing support. In this case, designers were involved in several projects and had limited resources available to assist after the system had been turned over to the end user. This problem could have been avoided by using a COTS system.

zeile.summary: System testing of the Space Shuttle Orbiter Avionics systems is typically done vie hard-line umbilicals. Since the umbilicals are no longer attached to the spacecraft at T-0, it is imperative that RF testing be performed with an integrated vehicle before a terminal countdown.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-16

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
System testing of the Space Shuttle Orbiter Avionics systems is typically done vie hard-line umbilicals. Since the umbilicals are no longer attached to the spacecraft at T-0, it is imperative that RF testing be performed with an integrated vehicle before a terminal countdown.

Lesson:
Initial testing of RF Avionics should be performed at its element level and at the integrated vehicle level. The integrated vehicle test should be done as early as possible before a terminal countdown. This would allow screening of failures caused by handling (closeout activities, lifting, or vibration). Early integrated RF testing would provide the opportunity to observe RF interference issues induced by other elements in the stack or external RF emitters (ground-based radios, WLAN devices, and tracking radars) that were introduced into the environment since previous processing flows.

zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-04-20

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Due to the high-volume storage of gases at KSC, gas leaks have often gone undetected for long periods. This resulted in significant costs, especially when there have been leaks in the gaseous helium (GHe) system. To detect a leak suspected in a large interconnected system such as the GHe system, subsystems must be incrementally isolated to narrow the leak down to a particular area for more focused, detailed inspections. This entails significant time and effort and, because outages in real time are required, also adds to the processing time.  New designs or upgrades to the KSC pneumatic systems should incorporate a strategy for detection and quick isolation of gas leakages.

Lesson:
The event described above is only one recent example of several GHe leak events that have occurred over the duration of the Shuttle program. Some of the known leak incidences have cost as much as $200,000 for a single event.  Over the long term of a program, significant savings could be achieved by better detection of gas leakages. For inert gases such as GN2, system leak detection working in conjunction with O2 monitoring systems, could also aid in safety enhancements.

zeile.title: Space Shuttle Propulsion Systems Ground Processing Lessons Learned
zeile.summary: Today�s space vehicle propulsion systems are complex, have many interfaces, and are costly to operate. New technologies are being developed to significantly reduce the inefficiencies built into today�s systems. The Operationally Efficient Propulsion System Study (OEPSS) was initiated by NASA in April 1989 to identify operations problems and cost drivers for current propulsion systems and to identify technology and design approaches to increase the operational efficiency and reduce operations cos [...]
zeile.content: Datum: 2010-05-19 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): Today�s space vehicle propulsion systems are complex, have many interfaces, and are costly to operate. New technologies are being developed to significantly reduce the inefficiencies built into today�s systems. The Operationally Efficient Propulsion System Study (OEPSS) was initiated by NASA in April 1989 to identify operations problems and cost drivers for current propulsion systems and to identify technology and design approaches to increase the operational efficiency and reduce operations cost for future propulsion systems. The results of the OEPSS were included in four data books: The OEPSS Data Book Volume I provided ground operations data. The OEPSS Data Book Volume II provided a definition of the 25 propulsion-related ground operations problems. The OEPSS Data Book Volume III provided operations technologies that could improve ground processing of propulsion systems. The OEPSS Data Book Volume IV provided design concepts for new space vehicle propulsion systems. These four data books are intended for use by designers/developers of future space launch vehicles. Lesson: Servicing the Space Shuttle propulsion systems required too many people and too much time, at a high cost. NASA/KSC performed the Operationally Efficient Propulsion System Study (OEPSS) to document major operational problems or concerns with the design of these propulsion systems. The study documents 25 major operations problems. Starting with the most pervasive, they include the following: Closed aft compartment Hydraulic systems Ocean recovery/refurbishment Separate OMS/RCS Gimbal system Sophisticated heat shield GN2/GHe purge Excess interfaces The OEPSS study provides data related to inefficiencies in processing the Space Shuttle propulsion systems. OEPSS Data Book Volume I contains ground operations data. OEPSS Data Book Volume II defines the 25 propulsion-related ground operations problems. OEPSS Data Book Volume III contains operations technologies that could improve ground processing of propulsion systems. And finally, OEPSS Data Book Volume IV provides design concepts for new space vehicle propulsion systems. In summary, the study identified existing or needed technologies that would improve processing efficiencies if applied to new systems during development.

zeile.title: Component Barcoding and Tracking Systems
zeile.summary: The processing of flight hardware requires the ability to track and account for thousands of individual parts in real time. Faster, more accurate processing and documentation can be achieved by applying a unique and intelligent bar-code label to each part, and tracking the parts in a central database. Travelers/part tags can be machine-printed and attached to parts so they can be tracked as they are removed, inspected, stored, recalled, and reinstalled.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-04-19 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The processing of flight hardware requires the ability to track and account for thousands of individual parts in real time. Faster, more accurate processing and documentation can be achieved by applying a unique and intelligent bar-code label to each part, and tracking the parts in a central database. Travelers/part tags can be machine-printed and attached to parts so they can be tracked as they are removed, inspected, stored, recalled, and reinstalled. Lesson: The discrepancies noted during return-to-flight processing included difficulty in producing a legible ID with rubber stamps and ink; illegible part/serial/order control numbers; human error in reading part/serial/order control numbers whether legible or not; and human error in transcribing part/serial/order control numbers onto paperwork. Other problems were noted, including time-consuming efforts in inventory control and reporting functions; mundane repetitive accountability procedures; the need for more stringent requirements for accuracy and quality control; and problems with configuration control and documentation control.

The lesson learned from this experience was that entering data by visual observation and handwritten entries produced numerous errors; but by bar-coding parts, a database can be built and used for easy processing of thousands of parts. Travelers can be printed with preloaded information from the database in lieu of making visual observations and hand entries.

Some advantages gained from bar coding and tracking were; Reduced cost (fewer installation mistakes per configuration and fewer installation man-hours) Improved accountability of hardware from removal through installation during processing (better logistic accountability and elimination of delays for configuration verification) Improved installation of parts (for multiple items) by bar-coding the part and its location with the same bar code number Improved efficiency _ rather than being retrieved from a random handwritten log, with the Parts To Go function, parts can be retrieved from a sorted list (arranged by vehicle zone, installation drawing, or any manner the technician might choose) Reduced need for paperwork to correct configuration discrepancies (errors in entering, reading, or transcribing part/serial/order control numbers) Reduced human error (in installation, reading ID labels, location, storage, and typographical errors) Use of common software to support both the TCS tracking system and Carrier Panel Tracking System.

The use of time-cycle intervals (such as a 360-day interval) for equipment maintenance is more applicable to ground support equipment (GSE) components that degrade within a given interval than to Operations Maintenance Requirement Systems Document (OMRSD) File VI maintenance requirements. zeile.title: Benefits Of Using A Traveler Tag Versus A Parts Tag On Removed Parts
zeile.summary: The Thermal Control System (TCS) tracking system has been in use since 1989 under the Shuttle Processing Data Management System II (SPDMS2). It was enhanced in 1992 to support the first Orbiter Maintenance Downtime Period (OMDP) for the Shuttle Orbiter Discovery (OV-103) at KSC and reduced processing rates to 33 TCS blankets in 15 minutes, with a program savings estimated at $90K per flow. In 2006, a conversion from the original LSOC1 program to Oracle brought many more enhanced features. This s [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-04-27 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The Thermal Control System (TCS) tracking system has been in use since 1989 under the Shuttle Processing Data Management System II (SPDMS2). It was enhanced in 1992 to support the first Orbiter Maintenance Downtime Period (OMDP) for the Shuttle Orbiter Discovery (OV-103) at KSC and reduced processing rates to 33 TCS blankets in 15 minutes, with a program savings estimated at $90K per flow. In 2006, a conversion from the original LSOC1 program to Oracle brought many more enhanced features. This system greatly enhanced processing of over 35,000 parts in the TCS inventory, both in the vehicles and in Logistics.

Under the previous system, a Work Authorization Document (WAD) had to be altered for each unique part. The WAD provided basic instructions that met the minimum installation requirements, but did not deal with issues specific to the individual part being installed. During high-volume parts processing (involving thousands of TCS blankets and their supporting structures or carrier panels), it was noted that the part tag did not contain all of the information and detailed requirements necessary. As a solution, a new type of part tag, called a �traveler,� was developed. With the traveler, the tracking system can fill in the data for each unique part without the need for a separate WAD. The traveler contains all the basic information found in a part tag, plus the additional information needed for tracking and processing. During processing, a removed part is tagged to identify its part number, serial number, and condition, and space is provided for a quality inspection stamp and date. Information on the authorizing document and next higher assembly may also be entered. Lesson: Although using part tags works well if a single item or a handful of items is being processed, it does not work well when a large number are being processed. To use part tags in high-volume processing, the WAD must either contain detailed steps for each part or a matrix must be used to ensure each part�s requirements are met.

For the new process, each part was assigned a unique bar code, a database was created with information on each part, and a new form (the blanket traveler) then captured any additional information or requirements pertaining to the bar codes associated with it. The traveler was developed to replace both the part tag and the IPD sheet.

Travelers offer a number of advantages over part tags. The traveler captures the detailed installation requirements from the drawing. It details the condition of each part, as well as the state (installation, etc.) of the part. It also contains buy-offs for all steps required to process the part (e.g., removal, inspection, approval to install, completion of installation, torque, and grounding). Unlike part tags, travelers can associate a part with a particular vehicle, installation drawing, or zone, or with a WAD for removal/installation; reflect when a part is installed; and show the final location of the part. The traveler may include references to Material Review (MR) conditions and reference the MR WAD number or one-of-a-kind work steps and buys.

A traveler�s information can be readily updated or corrected, and the information for the specific part can be printed.

zeile.title: Oxidizer Toxic Vapor Scrubber Eruption
zeile.summary: When large quantities of nitrogen tetroxide were processed at Launch Pad 39A, the oxidizer scrubber malfunctioned and erupted through the vent stack, spewing debris and caustic chemicals into the environment. Investigation revealed that the combination of sodium sulfite (Na2SO3) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH) used in the scrubber liquor caused a rapid exothermic reaction when an oxidizer leak caused the scrubber liquor to become saturated. The resulting steam caused an overpressure condition and re [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-12

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
When large quantities of nitrogen tetroxide were processed at Launch Pad 39A, the oxidizer scrubber malfunctioned and erupted through the vent stack, spewing debris and caustic chemicals into the environment. Investigation revealed that the combination of sodium sulfite (Na2SO3) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH) used in the scrubber liquor caused a rapid exothermic reaction when an oxidizer leak caused the scrubber liquor to become saturated. The resulting steam caused an overpressure condition and resulted in vent stack eruption. Changing the chemical make-up of the scrubber liquor has prevented recurrences of the incident.

Lesson:
Highly reactive chemicals, such as sodium sulfite and sodium hydroxide, may react differently when mixed in large quantities with an oxidizer as compared to small-scale laboratory tests.

zeile.title: Hardware Interface Module (HIM) Power Assembly Reliability
zeile.summary: The lack of visibility during the design process and the inability to inspect drawings for the HIM Power Assembly (HPA), an element of the Hardware Interface Module (HIM) resulted in numerous product modifications to address both safety and reliability issues _ one of which resulted in a fire in an HPA in Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF) 3. Active involvement by end item sustainers into the vendor design and production processes would have minimized these issues.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-02 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The lack of visibility during the design process and the inability to inspect drawings for the HIM Power Assembly (HPA), an element of the Hardware Interface Module (HIM) resulted in numerous product modifications to address both safety and reliability issues _ one of which resulted in a fire in an HPA in Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF) 3. Active involvement by end item sustainers into the vendor design and production processes would have minimized these issues. Lesson: The primary lessons learned from this experience are that improper vetting and subsequent monitoring of a contractor can lead to numerous and significant issues later.

The second contractor was selected by the first contractor and the visibility to both NASA and USA was extremely limited from the very beginning. After the initial contract was cancelled and the production contract for HIMs (which are the system that the HPAs supported) was awarded to a third company, their position was that this was a commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) item to them since NASA directed them to use this LRU. It was only after the quality and workmanship issues became known (and the subsequent IG investigation) that the numerous issues with the HPA would have to be addressed. The inaccuracy of the drawings and inconsistency with respect to the workmanship within the HPAs were merely symptoms of the overall problems with the processes at the second contractor.

zeile.title: Don't Let Reoccurring Issues Become the Norm
zeile.summary: In the environment surrounding the processing of space vehicles, it becomes very easy for people who work closely with the flight hardware to begin accepting recurring discrepancies as a normal part of flight operations, especially when those discrepancies occur within their own systems. In many cases, the discrepancy arises from problems with a different system, and there is a lack of communication between the system owners.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-15

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
In the environment surrounding the processing of space vehicles, it becomes very easy for people who work closely with the flight hardware to begin accepting recurring discrepancies as a normal part of flight operations, especially when those discrepancies occur within their own systems. In many cases, the discrepancy arises from problems with a different system, and there is a lack of communication between the system owners.

Lesson:
Any recurring discrepancy or nonconformance should never be treated as normal. Recurrence control procedures and guidelines should be put into place and used.

zeile.title: RMS Shoulder Brace Anomaly
zeile.summary: During STS-119 ground processing, a functional test of the Remote Manipulator System (RMS) was performed in accordance with OMI V1175, RMS Turnaround Verification, to ensure that all RMS hardware was ready for flight. The RMS shoulder brace was cycled and left in the latched position for flight. The required visual inspection for quality verification was reported as nominal. During the on-orbit checkout, the shoulder brace was released for operation. It was during this release that the crew repo [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-12

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
During STS-119 ground processing, a functional test of the Remote Manipulator System (RMS) was performed in accordance with OMI V1175, RMS Turnaround Verification, to ensure that all RMS hardware was ready for flight. The RMS shoulder brace was cycled and left in the latched position for flight. The required visual inspection for quality verification was reported as nominal. During the on-orbit checkout, the shoulder brace was released for operation. It was during this release that the crew reported a quicker than expected release (2 seconds instead of 5 to 8 seconds). Troubleshooting revealed that the requirements used to verify the shoulder brace latch prior to flight were not as accurate as thought. Historically, console program VAB40 was used to provide the data for the shoulder pitch angle prior to latching the shoulder brace. The requirement for shoulder pitch angle was 0.0 � 0.1 degrees in order to latch. Troubleshooting revealed that the pitch angle must be 0.0 � 0.07 degrees in order for the shoulder brace collet to engage. VAB40 only provided a resolution of one decimal place. Orbiter Display Page SPEC 169 provides a higher resolution of two decimal places and will be used for all future shoulder brace latch verifications. Lesson Learned: Ensure that the requirements can be supported by the actual testing and that the required resolution can be obtained from the specified data points.

Lesson:
A shoulder pitch angle of 0.0 � 0.1 degrees is necessary for the shoulder brace to latch. Historically, VAB40 console display has been used to verify this requirement. Troubleshooting revealed that if the shoulder pitch angle is more than 0.07 degrees, the collet will not engage the plate. Therefore, the RMS recommended action is to verify the shoulder pitch angle prior to latching the shoulder brace. The shoulder pitch angle must be 0.0 � 0.07 degrees, instead of the previously used angle requirement of � 0.1 degrees. Because of the lower resolution (one decimal place), VAB40 will no longer be used for this verification. Instead, RMS will use Orbiter Display Page SPEC 169 to verify joint angles because of the two-decimal-place resolution.

Lesson:
Helicoil locking devices can cause problems in applications requiring repeated engagements of the locking feature.          Potential problems, associated with temporary screw insertions into helicoils, can be minimized if shorter lubricated screws are used to assure minimal penetration of the locking mechanism.

zeile.summary: Door interfaces require a thermal seal that must be flexible and soft yet handle temperatures as high as 2000 degrees Fahrenheit. Silica-glass-based fabrics are primarily used for this application. Heat cycles on these materials tend to make them stiff and brittle, resulting in parts that are susceptible to damage from both flight and processing operations. New ideas to address this design requirement need to be explored. For the Space Shuttle Program, configuration changes were made that greatl [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-17

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Door interfaces require a thermal seal that must be flexible and soft yet handle temperatures as high as 2000 degrees Fahrenheit. Silica-glass-based fabrics are primarily used for this application. Heat cycles on these materials tend to make them stiff and brittle, resulting in parts that are susceptible to damage from both flight and processing operations. New ideas to address this design requirement need to be explored. For the Space Shuttle Program, configuration changes were made that greatly improved process operability, but the basic design has remained unchanged. From stand-point of flight safety, a single thermal barrier does not supply redundancy, and that risk must be accepted.

Lesson:
The soft goods necessary to seal door interfaces are very susceptible to wear and tear and require a high level of maintenance. Finding an alternative method to seal door interfaces should be a priority. If this is not feasible, then design changes should be made to ease processing efforts.

zeile.title: Impurities in Propellant-Grade Ammonia Can Lead to Corrosion and Poor Hardware Performance
zeile.summary: Leaks in the Space Shuttle ammonia boiler system, as well as a single instance of a boiler shutdown during postflight operation, led to a review of the materials and processes used in the ammonia boiler. Failure analysis was performed and concluded that the corrosion was caused by high levels of chloride in the procured ammonia and that the shutdown was due to high levels of polyethylene oxide (PEO) in the propellant-grade ammonia. Since the switch to higher-purity, technical-grade ammonia, ther [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-18

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Leaks in the Space Shuttle ammonia boiler system, as well as a single instance of a boiler shutdown during postflight operation, led to a review of the materials and processes used in the ammonia boiler. Failure analysis was performed and concluded that the corrosion was caused by high levels of chloride in the procured ammonia and that the shutdown was due to high levels of polyethylene oxide (PEO) in the propellant-grade ammonia. Since the switch to higher-purity, technical-grade ammonia, there have been no ammonia boiler leaks or shutdowns.

Lesson:
High levels of chlorides in propellant-grade ammonia attack the base metal of the boiler (347 stainless steel) and initiate pitting corrosion. Moisture provides the required electrolyte to support the corrosion process. In addition, the propellant-grade ammonia had higher levels of other contaminants, specifically polyethylene oxide (PEO). The PEO is a plasticizer that can clog heat exchanger passages, significantly reducing performance.

zeile.title: Dome Heat Shield Alignment Tool
zeile.summary: A simple tool consisting of a tapered bolt, a nut, and two close-tolerance "hat" bushings can be used to align two holes, without the use of undesired force.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-17 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): A simple tool consisting of a tapered bolt, a nut, and two close-tolerance "hat" bushings can be used to align two holes, without the use of undesired force. Lesson: A simple shop aid can align holes, without the application of force to the lifting fixture. The Dome Heat Shield Alignment Tool consists of a hardened-steel bolt with a 5-degree tapered shank, two close-tolerance brass "hat" bushings (one for the hole in the Orbiter [base heat shield] and the other for the hole in the dome heat shield), and a steel hex nut (free of all locking features). As the nut is turned, one of the bushings rides up the taper on the bolt, and the holes align. Fasteners are then installed in the holes adjacent to (i.e., above and below) the hole with the tool. When the tool is removed, the center hole remains aligned. A running torque restriction limits the forces. The tool has been used with great success on all the Orbiters.

Dome Heat Shield Alignment Tool used for alignment of holes

zeile.title: Missing Washers During Orbiter Ferry
zeile.summary: In 1997, part of the aft attaching hardware used for the Space Shuttle orbiter�s ferry flights was not installed during an orbiter/Shuttle Carrier Aircraft (SCA) mate operation, and the orbiter was ferried to Palmdale, CA, for an Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in a nonconforming configuration. It is essential to provide a secondary means of verification, such as a borescope inspection, of all critical hardware installations to verify that correct hardware is installed.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-08 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): In 1997, part of the aft attaching hardware used for the Space Shuttle orbiter�s ferry flights was not installed during an orbiter/Shuttle Carrier Aircraft (SCA) mate operation, and the orbiter was ferried to Palmdale, CA, for an Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in a nonconforming configuration. It is essential to provide a secondary means of verification, such as a borescope inspection, of all critical hardware installations to verify that correct hardware is installed. Lesson: Although the work steps to install the aft ferry-flight attach hardware were witnessed by the technicians, quality inspectors, and NASA, the installation of the conical washers was overlooked. The washers were not installed, causing the spherical washer chamfer to bind on the stress relief radius of the bolt shank to the head. After the hardware was removed from the SCA/orbiter, a missing part was identified as the MD153-5004-0032 washer from drawing M072-560001-018 (Ref Zone 63G). Spherical bearing V074-560106-002 was swaged/galled onto the bolt V074-560125-001 on the left-hand side, but the right-hand bearing was not swaged in place.

In addition, when torquing problems were encountered during installation of the flight attach hardware, the hardware should have been removed and inspected.

zeile.summary: Properly �spotting,� or accurately positioning, the Space Shuttle orbiter in the Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF) on the first roll-in attempt rarely occurred before the orbiter laser spotting system was put into use. The cost associated with delays was significant because employees had to wait for the spotting operation to be completed before they could begin work. In addition to the cost savings, a timely �spot� protected the orbiter and Shuttle workers from the elements when inclement weathe [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-08

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Properly �spotting,� or accurately positioning, the Space Shuttle orbiter in the Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF) on the first roll-in attempt rarely occurred before the orbiter laser spotting system was put into use. The cost associated with delays was significant because employees had to wait for the spotting operation to be completed before they could begin work. In addition to the cost savings, a timely �spot� protected the orbiter and Shuttle workers from the elements when inclement weather approached the OPF. This lesson describes the orbiter spotting system and the guidelines followed to use it successfully.

Lesson:
The orbiter laser spotting system became a very useful visual aid to spotting, although using it still relied on the experience and skill of its operators. The following guidelines were key to making it successful:       Determine the amount of correction needed by towing a short distance with the laser on the tug target centerline.      Apply the correction determined necessary and follow this new reference line on the target. Continue on a straight line using this new reference line without correcting for the NLG.      Upon reaching the forward jacks with the tug, make sure the RMLG laser is clearly within tolerance. If not, back out the orbiter completely and retry the spotting operation.      Once the tug clears the floor jacks, make the correction(s) needed to spot the NLG. The main landing gear (MLG) should remain within tolerance even with a significant NLG correction because of the short distance required to spot the NLG.

zeile.title: Bent Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) Pod Rotator
zeile.summary: The Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) pod rotator (a 5-ton jack screw) was bent on three occasions because of overloading. As a result, Boeing designed a system consisting of two load-sensing pins: one pin for attaching the rotator to the OMS pod lifting fixture and the other for attaching the rotator to the facility attachment point. Each sensing pin is connected to a readout unit to indicate when the rotator is under load or when the rotator load changes between tension and compre [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-04-21

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
The Space Shuttle Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) pod rotator (a 5-ton jack screw) was bent on three occasions because of overloading. As a result, Boeing designed a system consisting of two load-sensing pins: one pin for attaching the rotator to the OMS pod lifting fixture and the other for attaching the rotator to the facility attachment point. Each sensing pin is connected to a readout unit to indicate when the rotator is under load or when the rotator load changes between tension and compression. Two load-sensing pins are used for redundancy.

Lesson:
The rotator's screw shaft will bend if the rotator is overdriven. The rotator's screw shaft will also bend if the jack screws of the lifting-fixture pivot shaft are overdriven. The operating personnel used several different indicators to determine when the rotator was unloaded; however, all of the methods depended on feel or sight. Less experienced operating personnel were not always able to make the right call.

zeile.title: Space Shuttle Systems Life Cycle Cost Lessons Learned
zeile.summary: In 1991, NASA chartered a Space Propulsion Synergy Team (SPST) to improve communications between the users and developers for NASA programs. The SPST's first task was to compare the Space Shuttle's achievements to the original requirements, objectives, and goals of the Space Shuttle Program. The shortfalls were documented in two reports published by the SPST. The reports defined the lessons learned from the Space Shuttle Program related to the Program�s Life Cycle Cost (LCC) issues. The first re [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-21

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
In 1991, NASA chartered a Space Propulsion Synergy Team (SPST) to improve communications between the users and developers for NASA programs. The SPST's first task was to compare the Space Shuttle's achievements to the original requirements, objectives, and goals of the Space Shuttle Program. The shortfalls were documented in two reports published by the SPST. The reports defined the lessons learned from the Space Shuttle Program related to the Program�s Life Cycle Cost (LCC) issues. The first report is titled, "Current Space Shuttle System Shortfalls Assessment," revised October 18, 2005. The second report is titled, "Space Transportation Systems Life Cycle Cost Assessment and Control," revised March 5, 2009. Both of these reports are attached to this lessons learned report.

Lesson:
The SPST stated that a major lesson learned from their studies was that much-improved, innovative processes must be developed and rigorously applied to effectively control life cycle cost. The SPST also stated that NASA must balance the Safety, Reliability, and Maintainability requirements to provide controls on the burden of recurring maintenance, thus providing operational effectiveness and LCC. Finally, the SPST concluded that another major lessons learned was that systems requirements must be clearly defined, flowed down, and controlled during the design development and test evaluation phases of the program. The requirements must cover all major objectives, not just the performance objectives but also the operational requirements for the system to achieve sustainable life cycle costs.

zeile.title: Propellant Storage Tank Dual Relief Valves
zeile.summary: During an operation to remove and replace the oxidizer storage tank relief valve with a new calibrated relief valve, a technician ripped open his Self-Contained Atmospheric Ensemble (SCAPE) suit. During the intervening time when the technicians were evacuated, the open storage tank released an estimated 12,236 cubic feet of oxidizer vapor into the atmosphere. A number of personnel were exposed to the vapor in the downwind area.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-13 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): During an operation to remove and replace the oxidizer storage tank relief valve with a new calibrated relief valve, a technician ripped open his Self-Contained Atmospheric Ensemble (SCAPE) suit. During the intervening time when the technicians were evacuated, the open storage tank released an estimated 12,236 cubic feet of oxidizer vapor into the atmosphere. A number of personnel were exposed to the vapor in the downwind area. Lesson: Because there is no design to prevent the release of propellant when the storage tank relief valves are removed, effective scheduling of an operation to accomplish the removal is essential. Plan the task for winter when the propellant will be colder. Maintenance at temperatures below 68 �F on N2O4 storage system will greatly reduce the boil-off of N2O4.

Nominal maintenance items on hypergolic storage vessels that will require replacement or calibration should be designed in such a way that will allow maintenance or calibration to be done while not requiring major hazardous operations or the need to completely drain the storage vessel of propellant. Since ASME code does not allow an isolation valve in front of a relief valve, a design with more than one relief valve with a three-way isolation valve will allow compliance with the code and also allow isolation of one relief valve for maintenance.

In this design, the tank is always protected by a relief device and the design allows for the purging of the off-line relief valve pipe and the replacement of the relief valve as a minor hazardous operation. This design also allows for the annual calibration to be accomplished with the RV installed. Processing costs are reduced and personnel and the effect on the environment are controlled. The importance of effective and correct evaluation of outstanding ESRs is demonstrated in this case. If the effect on the environment of the annual replacement and the risk to personnel was correctly evaluated and acted upon, then this event could have been eliminated. Combine this with the proper planning of the calibration and implementation of the modification to occur during cold weather, and the amount of released propellant could have been minimized.

When Environmental Control System (ECS) purge support requirements for the Orbiter were originally developed, they identified the parameters of the purge and when a purge should be started and ended while the Orbiter was in different locations. Lesson:
If you plan to provide an ECS purge for long periods during spacecraft ground processing, it is better to have a requirement to cover unplanned purge outages and excursions from the beginning.

zeile.title: Development and Evolution of the Main Propulsion Helium Signature Test
zeile.summary: This lesson learned addresses the development and evolution of a test technique for revalidating the Space Shuttle Orbiter Main Propulsion System (MPS) during ground turnaround operations between flights. This test technique, the Helium Signature Test, is an end-to-end leak check of the entire MPS and serves as a final validation of flightworthiness. A test such as the Helium Signature Test can be used for any enclosed hazardous system with a control volume to ensure overall system integrity bef [...]
zeile.content: Datum: 2010-04-20 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): This lesson learned addresses the development and evolution of a test technique for revalidating the Space Shuttle Orbiter Main Propulsion System (MPS) during ground turnaround operations between flights. This test technique, the Helium Signature Test, is an end-to-end leak check of the entire MPS and serves as a final validation of flightworthiness. A test such as the Helium Signature Test can be used for any enclosed hazardous system with a control volume to ensure overall system integrity before the hazardous medium is introduced. Lesson: While point leak checks of individual threaded, flange, brazed, and welded joints are important validations of joint integrity for new and not-yet-validated joints, as well as good interval checks of the health of these components, they do not cover all possible sources of propellant leakage. Fatigue or wear during a previous flight or damage during ground processing could result in leakage from a component that was not leak-checked, or that was leak-checked before the damage occurred. An overall system leak check performed as close as possible to aft fuselage closeout for flight gives the best confidence that the system is ready to support safe flight.

zeile.summary: For many years Ground Support Equipment (GSE) was periodically proof loaded based on NSTS 08171, Operations and Maintenance Requirements and Specifications Documents (OMRSDs) File VI requirements. This caused premature wear of components, decreased safety, and increased time to perform maintenance. zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-26

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
For many years Ground Support Equipment (GSE) was periodically proof loaded based on NSTS 08171, Operations and Maintenance Requirements and Specifications Documents (OMRSDs) File VI requirements. This caused premature wear of components, decreased safety, and increased time to perform maintenance. Reliability Centered Maintenance (RCM) methodology was used to determine optimum maintenance tactics for GSE and flight assets.

Lesson:
Annual proof load testing could be replaced with nondestructive evaluation (NDE) inspection of the critical welds. Proof load of GSE can be replaced with visual/NDE inspections and rated load tests. KNPR 8715.3 provides a section for the nonload test of slings and lifting fixtures. In the case of the OMS pod handling fixture, it is 200% of rated load. In most other cases, it is 150%.

Abstract (Volltext):
The highly polished sealing surfaces of Dynatube fittings are susceptible to incurring defects across the sealing surfaces, which may result in a decrease in the ability to achieve a leak free joint. The probability of incurring a defect is compounded in designs with a limited envelope for access, or where repetitive disconnections/connections are required.  In applications where access for replacement is not feasible, i.e. where hazards exist, or an assessment of the risk for collateral system damage is high, an alternative method for repair is available.  The Dynatube �Seal Saver� developed by the Johnson Space Center, consists of a Teflon coated stainless steel ring, which can be inserted upon initial installation as a mitigation factor against subsequent damage, or when upon inspection, minor radial defects detected across the sealing surfaces would otherwise allow for a leak to propagate.

Lesson:
Dynatube fittings are a time proven dynamically acceptable fitting for space craft. It can be used in both propellant and high pressure clean gas design applications. Proper access should be afforded in the use of dynatube fittings for disconnection/connection and repetitive use.

zeile.title: Flame Trench Refractory Failure Modes
zeile.summary: The Fondu Fyre (a type of heat-resistant concrete) and brick materials used in the flame trench refractory at Launch Pad 39A were originally specified for the Apollo program, which had a different launch environment than the Space Shuttle program. When a large area of the refractory brick on the east surface of the flame trench failed during a launch in 2008, an investigation determined that future programs would need a better method for inspecting the launch trench refractory, a better definiti [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-06-01

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
The Fondu Fyre (a type of heat-resistant concrete) and brick materials used in the flame trench refractory at Launch Pad 39A were originally specified for the Apollo program, which had a different launch environment than the Space Shuttle program. When a large area of the refractory brick on the east surface of the flame trench failed during a launch in 2008, an investigation determined that future programs would need a better method for inspecting the launch trench refractory, a better definition of vehicle load requirements and environments, an analysis of new types of refractory materials, and a risk analysis for flame trench failure modes.

Lesson:
The fact that a legacy system has never failed catastrophically does not guarantee that it will not fail in the future. Vehicle load requirements and environments need to be defined when new launch vehicles are developed. If more comprehensive inspection methods had been used when material erosion was first becoming more noticeable in the flame trench, the failure�s impact on the program might have been lessened.

zeile.summary: Classically, Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) and System Assurance Analysis (SAA) have omitted passive elements of the design. These elements must be included to have a complete and effective maintenance plan and to avoid potential catastrophic failures.

Classically, Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) and System Assurance Analysis (SAA) have omitted passive elements of the design. These elements must be included to have a complete and effective maintenance plan and to avoid potential catastrophic failures.

Lesson:
Performing periodic tests and inspections of passive flight and ground support system elements such as wiring, mechanical fasteners, and pressurized tubing that support critical flight and ground support systems can help to avoid catastrophic failures of these systems.

zeile.title: Design for Operability;  High Use Nut Plate/ Insert Design
zeile.summary: Line-replaceable units (LRUs) are removed, replaced, or inspected far more often than related parts on a standard aircraft. The fastener receptacles quickly become worn and are often difficult to access or replace. For reusable spacecraft, nut plates should be designed for frequent use. Nylon-style locking features such as Vespel should be avoided.
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-07-16

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Line-replaceable units (LRUs) are removed, replaced, or inspected far more often than related parts on a standard aircraft. The fastener receptacles quickly become worn and are often difficult to access or replace. For reusable spacecraft, nut plates should be designed for frequent use. Nylon-style locking features such as Vespel should be avoided.

Lesson:
For reusable spacecraft, nut plates should be designed for frequent use. If a secondary locking feature is required, the locking feature should be placed on the bolt rather than on the insert or nut plate. Nylon-style locking features such as Vespel should be avoided because, on certain joints, the preload may be unstable during flight loads and thermal cycles.

zeile.summary: Some tasks can easily be taken for granted, particularly ones that seem straightforward and low-risk. During Shuttle processing, fasteners were often found to be improperly installed. Many conditions can lead to improper installation, which can have catastrophic results. Blind installations must be verified through an accurate assessment of the joint. Often tolerances stack up in multilayer joints. And countersinks can lead to unacceptable grip lengths, in turn resulting in shank-out conditions [...]
zeile.content: Datum: 2010-07-16 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): Some tasks can easily be taken for granted, particularly ones that seem straightforward and low-risk. During Shuttle processing, fasteners were often found to be improperly installed. Many conditions can lead to improper installation, which can have catastrophic results. Blind installations must be verified through an accurate assessment of the joint. Often tolerances stack up in multilayer joints. And countersinks can lead to unacceptable grip lengths, in turn resulting in shank-out conditions or insufficient thread engagement. Lesson: Accurate measurement of the grip length is critical to blind installation of fasteners. Many conditions, such as tolerance stack-up, washer configuration, and countersinks, can lead to a false or inaccurate determination of proper grip length.

zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-07-16 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): In November 2009, United Space Alliance published the "Constellation Launch Control System Operations Assessment Trade Study." This trade study highlighted many current and historical risks in the operation and maintenance of the Launch Processing System (LPS) for the retiring Space Shuttle program.

The primary goal of the document was to reduce program risk by presenting lessons learned from decades of processing experience to the designers of the Constellation Program as considerations in the development of the new Launch Control System (LCS).

The document is a compendium of 30 years of experience with the LPS. Lesson: The document presents 121 pages of findings, prioritized with regard to vehicle and GSE processing, daily operations, manpower, schedule, and cost. The Executive Summary identified the following key areas: Set redundancy requirements for safe operation Increased risk of concurrent operations Facility and vehicle data stream identifier tag requirements Configuration management risks Multiple set management risks Increased operational, security, and maintenance risks in virtualized command and control environments Human-computer interface/human-error prevention

zeile.title: Reinforced Carbon-Carbon (RCC) Inspection Processes
zeile.summary: Reinforced carbon-carbon (RCC) is a material that can withstand the high temperatures of reentry and can be used in areas where greater durability is desired. When RCC is exposed to high temperatures, it oxidizes rapidly, so a coating is required to reduce its exposure to oxygen. Reactions with these coatings can cause subsurface voids in the RCC. To accurately inspect and assess the condition of the RCC, a nondestructive evaluation (NDE) is required to see under the outside coatings. Thermograp [...]
zeile.content: Datum: 2010-07-19 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): Reinforced carbon-carbon (RCC) is a material that can withstand the high temperatures of reentry and can be used in areas where greater durability is desired. When RCC is exposed to high temperatures, it oxidizes rapidly, so a coating is required to reduce its exposure to oxygen. Reactions with these coatings can cause subsurface voids in the RCC. To accurately inspect and assess the condition of the RCC, a nondestructive evaluation (NDE) is required to see under the outside coatings. Thermography is one method that was utilized for RCC inspections. When using NDE as an inspection process, the criteria and baselines have to be well developed to accurately interpret the results so that indications are understood and an accurate assessment can be made to determine the acceptability of the condition observed. Lesson: Although NDE did provide a much better view of the subsurface conditions and should be used for this situation, it is equally important to perform a baseline study to calibrate the results. Voids and anomalies exist on brand new parts, and acceptance criteria must be developed based on testing.

zeile.title: Use of  Request for Specific Action (RSA) Database System in Space Shuttle Processing
zeile.summary: The Request for Specific Action (RSA) system developed for the Space Shuttle Thermal Protection System (TPS) provides technicians and quality inspectors an easy and direct way to identify concerns or to submit ideas for improving maintenance or repair procedures. The system tracks the request to ensure a cross-functional engineering team addresses all concerns and evaluates all suggestions for improvement. This system has identified specification deficiencies and has led to numerous process impr [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-07-19 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): The Request for Specific Action (RSA) system developed for the Space Shuttle Thermal Protection System (TPS) provides technicians and quality inspectors an easy and direct way to identify concerns or to submit ideas for improving maintenance or repair procedures. The system tracks the request to ensure a cross-functional engineering team addresses all concerns and evaluates all suggestions for improvement. This system has identified specification deficiencies and has led to numerous process improvements. Lesson: Numerous significant deficiencies were detected and addressed using the RSA system. The system was developed in a USA/Boeing/NASA collaborative effort and provides a simple Web-based method for technicians, inspectors, and systems engineers to quickly identify problems with the specification or to quickly suggest ways the specification could be improved.

The RSA system was developed with input fields that ask the initiator to provide a problem description as well as his/her suggested possible solution. The RSA is automatically assigned a tracking number and reviewed by an engineering team of system specialists that includes USA/Boeing and NASA. Any RSAs that have the potential to affect the safety of the vehicle or personnel are immediately elevated and further documentation initiated. Process enhancements are evaluated by the team and specification changes are coordinated and implemented.

This system has been highly effective in identifying and correcting specification deficiencies, as well as in incorporating specification and design improvements.

A launch can be delayed if the schedule does not account for this extra time for filling. Lesson: To avoid launch delays, the water lines in the Sound Suppression Water System should be prefilled before the start of the countdown.

zeile.summary:
Contamination control facility environmental Operational Maintenance Requirements and Specifications Document (OMRSD) requirements were created before it was determined if they were even achievable during normal Orbiter processing at the Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF) high bays, and before it was determined if they were really warranted to protect the cleanliness level of the exposed Orbiter Payload Bay.

After processing problem reports and waivers and/or exceptions to the OMRSD r [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-27 Organisation: KSC Abstract (Volltext): Contamination control facility environmental Operational Maintenance Requirements and Specifications Document (OMRSD) requirements were created before it was determined if they were even achievable during normal Orbiter processing at the Orbiter Processing Facility (OPF) high bays, and before it was determined if they were really warranted to protect the cleanliness level of the exposed Orbiter Payload Bay.

After processing problem reports and waivers and/or exceptions to the OMRSD requirements for a number of missions, it was determined that violating the OMRSD requirements during normal processing was not causing any obvious detrimental effects to the flight hardware from a contamination control perspective. Therefore, the facility OMRSD requirements were determined to be no longer warranted and were deleted per RCN KV9009M2. Lesson: Data collection during a number of Orbiter processing flows was necessary to determine which facility contamination control OMRSD requirements were truly warranted to achieve and/or maintain the required flight hardware cleanliness level. Those OMRSD requirements that were not warranted were deleted in accordance with RCN KV9009M2.

zeile.summary: Constraints, or the identification of a precedence order for work procedures, are crucial to flight hardware processing. A constraints system has been in place for many years in the Shuttle Program. However, when a new electronic work control system was brought online for Ares I-X processing, a robust and automated way of controlling constraints was not provided. As a result, several constraints were missed, and this drove the need to rework constraints, such as opening a closed-out area back up [...]
zeile.content:
Datum: 2010-05-01

Organisation: KSC

Abstract (Volltext):
Constraints, or the identification of a precedence order for work procedures, are crucial to flight hardware processing. A constraints system has been in place for many years in the Shuttle Program. However, when a new electronic work control system was brought online for Ares I-X processing, a robust and automated way of controlling constraints was not provided. As a result, several constraints were missed, and this drove the need to rework constraints, such as opening a closed-out area back up to complete work that was missed. This can even become a safety issue. A system must be put in place when new work control systems are brought online for the identification of a precedence order for work procedures.

Lesson:
Constraints management is critical to safe and efficient hardware processing. If a constraint system is not present, open work may not be completed. Therefore, a robust and automated constraints process is critical.
